name: Vienna Gambit
summary: The Vienna Gambit is an aggressive 1.e4 e5 weapon: after 2.Nc3 White plays an early f2-f4, a King's Gambit where the c3-knight already guards e4. Against 2...Nf6 3.f4 the critical 3...d5 4.fxe5 Nxe4 5.Qf3 leads to sharp but balanced play, while the natural 3...exf4? is punished by 4.e5!, which sends the f6-knight back home. Black's other replies (3...Nc6, 3...Bc5, 3...Bb4) run into fxe5 and quick tactics, so the opening scores very well at club level.
keyIdeas: 2.Nc3 keeps the f-pawn free: f2-f4 attacks e5 and opens the f-file for our rook and queen.
If Black takes on f4 with the knight on f6, e4-e5 kicks it - ...Nh5 and ...Ng4 lose to Qxh5/Qxg4 on the d1-h5 diagonal, so it must go back to g8.
After 3...d5 4.fxe5 Nxe4, the e5-pawn is our trump: it cramps Black and takes f6 and d6 from Black's pieces.
5.Qf3 attacks the e4-knight twice; Bb5 pins a knight on c6 so it can neither take e5 nor defend.
Watch Black's ...Qh4+ trick in every line: g3, Nf3 (covers h4) or Qf2 (blocks the diagonal) are the standard antidotes.
Against ...Bc5 or ...Bb4 setups, look for fxe5 and the Qg4 fork on g7 and loose knights.
If queens are traded, Black's doubled c-pawns and our open f-file give us the easier endgame.
typicalPlans: Regain the f4-pawn with Nf3, d4 and Bxf4, then castle long and attack with the queen on the e-file.
In the 5.Qf3 lines, put a rook on the f-file or b-file and play against Black's damaged queenside pawns.
Against passive ...d6 setups, build the centre with Nf3, d4 and play for the e4-e5 break.
In the Hamppe-Allgaier, give the knight on f7, then play d4, Bxf4, g3/Bg2 and O-O with the f-file aimed at the black king.
commonMistakes: Grabbing on e4 too early: after 5.Qf3 Nc6, 6.Nxe4? Nd4! hits the queen and c2.
Forgetting ...Qh4+: always check whether the h4-e1 diagonal is open before moving the f-pawn or king's knight.
Retreating the queen when the knight leaves e4: after 5...Ng5 the right move is 6.Qxd5!, winning a pawn.
Taking with the queen when a knight can take: after 3...Bc5 4.fxe5 Nxe4, play 5.Nxe4, not 5.Qg4.
Playing the Hamppe-Allgaier without knowing 8...f3!: Black can return the pawn to open the g-file - know the ideas or choose 3.Bc4.

lines.name: Main line: 5.Qf3 Nc6 6.Bb5 (Paulsen Attack)
lines.description: The critical test of 5.Qf3. Black counterattacks with 5...Nc6, we pin it with 6.Bb5 and after 6...Nxc3 7.dxc3 Qh4+ 8.g3 Qe4+ an equal but unbalanced endgame arises where Black's doubled c-pawns and our active rook give us the easier play. Other 6th moves: 6...Be6 7.Nge2 (develop, keep the pin), 6...Qh4+ 7.g3 Qe7 8.d4 (Black's queen blocks the f8-bishop), 6...Bd7 7.Nxe4 dxe4 8.Qxe4 (we win a pawn) and 6...Bf5?? 7.Qxf5 (see the trap line). 5...Be6 is met by 6.Nxe4 dxe4 7.Qxe4 Nc6 8.Nf3 with an extra pawn to defend. The rare 2...Bb4 is answered by 3.Nf3 Nf6 4.Nxe5 O-O 5.Nd3 with a small edge.
lines.evaluation: Equal endgame (about -0.1); White has the more active rook, Black the bishop pair.

lines.name: 5.Qf3 Nxc3 6.bxc3 Be7 7.d4 c5

lines.name: Trap: 5.Qf3 Ng5? 6.Qxd5!
lines.description: 5...Ng5 attacks our queen, but moving the knight off e4 opens the f3-d5 diagonal: the d5-pawn is attacked by the queen and the c3-knight and defended only once. lines.name: Alternative: 5.Nf3 Be7 6.Qe2 (Breyer Variation)
lines.description: The classical 5.Nf3 is a calmer alternative to 5.Qf3: we develop, guard e5 and prepare d4. In the Breyer Variation White castles long and attacks with h4. Black is fine with accurate play, which is why 5.Qf3 is our main move. Black's other 5th moves (5...Bc5 6.d4 Bb4 7.Bd2, 5...c5 6.Bb5+ Nc6 7.O-O, 5...a6 6.d3, 5...Be6 6.Qe2, 5...Bf5 6.d3) follow the same plan: hit e4, develop and use the f-file. After 6.Qe2, 6...f5 7.d3, 6...Ng5 7.d4 and 6...Bf5 7.Nd4 are all roughly level.
lines.evaluation: About equal; Black is slightly more comfortable (-0.4) but the position is rich.

lines.name: Trap: 5.d3 Qh4+ 6.g3 (Wurzburger Trap)
lines.description: 5.d3 (the Oxford Variation) kicks the knight at once. lines.evaluation: After 11...Bxc2? 12.b3 Black has given a bishop for two pawns (about +3 for White); with best play the line is equal.

lines.description: Taking the pawn is the most common reply at club level, but after 4.e5 the f6-knight has no good square and must go back to g8. lines.evaluation: White wins the queen for a knight (about +7).

lines.description: The solid 3...d6 keeps the f6-knight and leads to King's Gambit Declined-type play. After 4.Nf3 Nc6 5.Bb5 the pin means fxe5 is a real threat.
